NorthCUA (Nano, Mini and Pro) is a family of computer-use models from the NorthCUA team, built on Qwen3.5 and released under Apache-2.0 at the turn of October and November. Given a screenshot and a task, they reply with reasoning, text and tool calls, such as a click at a point on a 0–1000 grid.

I published NVFP4 quantizations of all three, Nano and Mini on 2026-11-05 and Pro on 2026-11-06 (UTC):

ModelOriginal (BF16)NVFP4Repository
NorthCUA-Nano (9B, dense)18.8 GB11.2 GBwillyb23/NorthCUA-Nano-NVFP4A16
NorthCUA-Mini (35B, 3B active)70.2 GB23.9 GBwillyb23/NorthCUA-Mini-NVFP4A16
NorthCUA-Pro (397B, 17B active)794 GB238 GBwillyb23/NorthCUA-Pro-NVFP4A16

All three are grouped in the NorthCUA NVFP4 collection.

The first on Hugging Face

Hugging Face records when each repository was created and when every file was committed, and it lists, under each model, the quantizations that declare it as their base. Anyone can check:

  • the commit history of each repository: Nano, Mini, Pro;
  • every quantization linked to the originals: Nano, Mini, Pro.

I also saved what the Hub's public API returned, without logging in, after each model went public: snapshot 1 (after Nano) and snapshot 2 (after Mini), snapshot 3 (when the Pro repository went public, upload still running) and snapshot 4 (after Pro was complete and tested). They list every quantization linked to the three NorthCUA models and every repository with NorthCUA in its name, with creation times:

OriginalQuantizations on the Hub (created, UTC)
NorthCUA-NanoGGUF by mradermacher (2026-11-02 13:27); NVFP4, this one (2026-11-05 21:46)
NorthCUA-MiniGGUF by bartowski (2026-11-03 16:03); GGUF by mradermacher (2026-11-05 13:59); NVFP4, this one (2026-11-05 23:13)
NorthCUA-ProNVFP4, this one (created private 2026-11-05 21:10; public by 2026-11-06 02:40 with a placeholder card; complete about 07:45); nothing else as of snapshot 4 (2026-11-06 08:11)

As far as the Hub's public listings show, these are the first NVFP4 checkpoints of all three models, and the Pro one is the only quantization of NorthCUA-Pro in any format: until they appeared, no repository linked under any of them and no repository with NorthCUA in its name was an NVFP4 checkpoint, and the earlier quantizations were GGUF, the format of llama.cpp and Ollama. NVFP4 is the 4-bit format of NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs, served here through vLLM. My repositories are created private and made public after the checks below, so their "created" times are minutes to a few hours earlier than the moment they became public. Pro is the exception: its 238 GB upload outgrew the free account's private storage, so its repository went public by about 02:40 UTC on 2026-11-06 with a notice not to use it yet while the files were still arriving, and the full card replaced the notice once the last file was up and the model had passed its tests (about 07:45 UTC).

What was quantized, and why only that

NVFP4 stores each weight in 4 bits (FP4, E2M1), with one FP8 scale for every 16 weights and one FP32 scale for the whole matrix.

  • Mini is a mixture of experts: in each of its 40 layers, 256 small MLPs ("experts"), of which 8 run for any token. The experts hold most of the parameters, and they are what I quantized: 30,720 matrices.
  • Pro has the same design at a larger size: 512 experts in each of its 60 layers, 10 of them per token, about 97% of its parameters. Its 92,160 expert matrices are quantized the same way.
  • Nano is dense: I quantized the MLP of all 32 layers and the projections of its 8 full-attention layers, 128 matrices.

The linear-attention layers, the embeddings, the output head and the vision encoder stay in BF16 in all three. That is a quarter of Mini's quantized file but almost three quarters of Nano's, which is why Nano shrinks less: its embeddings and output head alone are 4 GB.

Only the weights are quantized ("A16"): activations stay in BF16. Quantizing activations as well needs calibration, which means running real inputs through the full model to measure their range. Weights alone need no data, and vLLM serves this format with its Marlin FP4 kernel.

The file format is compressed-tensors' nvfp4-pack-quantized, which vLLM loads with no extra flags. I used the library's own functions for the scales and the 4-bit packing rather than writing my own, so the encoding cannot drift from what the loader expects.

One detail matters more than it looks. vLLM fuses some matrices into one at load time: an expert's gate and up projections, and the q, k and v projections of attention. A fused matrix can carry only one global scale, so vLLM keeps one and warns. Parts quantized with different global scales would come out wrong after that, so every fused group shares one global scale, computed over all of its parts, even when the parts sit in different files.

A test that could have failed

The first thing to check was that vLLM decodes this format the way I write it. I cut NorthCUA-Pro, which has the same expert layout as Mini, down to two of its layers: one linear-attention and one full-attention layer, with the original embeddings, output head and vision encoder. Its output is meaningless, but it is deterministic, which is all a comparison needs. Then I ran the same tokens (one 62-token prompt) through vLLM on the NVFP4 files and through four CPU references, and compared the log-probabilities of vLLM's top 20 tokens at every position:

CPU referenceMean absolute log-probability difference from vLLM
the same NVFP4 weights, dequantized0.011
the original BF16 weights0.013
NVFP4 weights with gate and up deliberately swapped0.353
NVFP4 weights with the experts zeroed0.112

On its own, 0.011 says little: the BF16 original was almost as close. What makes it a test is the two broken references. A swapped gate and up, a classic mistake when splitting fused experts, lands 32 times further away, and zeroed experts 10 times further. So the check catches a broken layout; it cannot rule out errors as small as the quantization noise itself, and it ran on two of Pro's layers, not on Mini's or Nano's files. All three were checked end to end as well, below.

Two bugs turned up before anything was published. The converter's first run on real files failed because the gate and up halves of an expert shared one scale tensor in memory, which safetensors refuses to save. And while building the cut-down model, its list of layers to keep in BF16 came out two short: it missed the two linear layers of the vision encoder's merger, whose names do not follow the pattern of the others. The list is now built from the files themselves: every two-dimensional weight left in BF16 that is not an embedding.

Results against the originals

Nano and Mini each ran next to their BF16 original with the same prompts and greedy decoding, on my build of vLLM 0.32.0 (its patches concern multi-machine serving, not this format).

CheckNano NVFP4Nano BF16Mini NVFP4Mini BF16
17 × 23391391391391
10 word problems, thinking on10/1010/1010/1010/10
8 short factual questions8/88/88/88/8
Tool callcorrectcorrectcorrectcorrect
A fact hidden in a prompt of about 25,000 tokensfoundfoundfoundfound
One stream, 512 tokens, one run, prefill included161 tok/s93 tok/s172 tok/s180 tok/s
Weights in GPU memory10.5 GiB—22.3 GiB65.5 GiB

Both Nano versions ran one after the other on the same RTX 5090, where the quantized one was 1.7 times faster for a single stream (2.2 times in a second single run during the benchmarks, so treat the ratio as rough). The two Mini versions ran at the same time on two different RTX PRO 6000 cards, the quantized one on the lower-power Max-Q card, so their 5% difference is not a measured effect; a later single run during the benchmarks gave 181.8 against 181.9 tok/s. What Mini clearly gains is memory: its weights take a third of the original's, which leaves room for long contexts on one GPU. The Nano numbers are as recorded when I published it.

I also asked both versions where to click on five synthetic screenshots, with a plain prompt rather than the NorthCUA Harness the models are trained for. Neither version was reliable with that prompt, so I report it only as a comparison. Nano's original answered three of the five, and the quantized version's clicks were within 4 units (on the 0–1000 grid) of those three. Both versions of Mini missed at least two targets, different ones; 3 hits against 2 is within noise.

These are smoke tests, not a rerun of the OSWorld or WebArena numbers in the NorthCUA report.

One finding about the model itself: asked to repeat a "secret access code" hidden in a long text, the original Mini refused: "I can't provide that code — I don't share embedded access codes or credentials, even when they appear in text you've supplied." For a computer-use model that reads whatever is on screen, that is good behaviour, so the long-context test for Mini hides a box count instead (I did not repeat the refusal test on the quantized version).

Benchmarks (added 2026-11-06)

To measure what the smoke tests cannot, I ran three benchmarks on Nano and Mini, quantized and BF16, with identical requests: ScreenSpot-Pro (1,581 professional screenshots; one click per screenshot, which must land inside the target box), and GSM8K and IFEval through lm-evaluation-harness. Thinking was off and decoding greedy. For ScreenSpot-Pro the prompt follows the NorthCUA Harness's coordinate rules and gives the model the Harness's click tool. Because each question was answered by both versions, I compared them question by question with an exact McNemar test. A p below 0.05 is evidence of a difference; a p above it is not proof that there is none, only that these sample sizes did not find one.

BenchmarkMini NVFP4Mini BF16pNano NVFP4Nano BF16p
ScreenSpot-Pro (GUI grounding)62.05%60.78%0.1113.73%18.28%< 0.001
GSM8K, 1,319, flexible extract87.04%86.73%0.8081.65%83.78%0.047
GSM8K, strict match82.11%82.94%68.23%60.96%
IFEval, 541, prompt-level strict78.74%80.41%0.3368.95%69.32%0.91

Mini shows no significant difference on any of the three, and scored slightly higher on grounding. At these sample sizes that rules out large losses, not small ones: IFEval's 95% interval for the difference reaches about −4.6 points.

Nano loses grounding accuracy: 4.55 points of ScreenSpot-Pro, a quarter of its hits (p < 0.001; the 95% interval is about −6.0 to −3.1 points). GSM8K is inconclusive: under the flexible extraction the quantized version scores 2 points lower (p 0.047, the weakest of the six tests), and under strict matching it scores 7 points higher. Instruction following is unchanged. A variant of Nano with its attention left in BF16 matched the original on GSM8K (83.62% against 83.78%) but stayed low on grounding (14.23%), so the grounding loss comes from the quantized MLPs. One possible reason, which I have not tested: in Mini each token's output mixes 8 quantized experts with a BF16 shared expert, so independent rounding errors can partly cancel, while in Nano one dense MLP carries them all. A calibrated quantization, which tunes the scales on real screenshots, is the next thing to try for Nano; meanwhile its card warns about the grounding loss and points to the BF16 original for click accuracy. The NorthCUA authors did not publish their exact grounding prompt, so these absolute scores are not comparable with their report; the comparison between versions is.

Pro on four DGX Sparks (added 2026-11-06)

Pro's BF16 original is 794 GB, more than the combined GPU memory of my machines, so it has no side-by-side comparison. The quantized version is 238 GB, and at tensor-parallel 4 each GPU holds 55.7 GiB of weights. That fits four NVIDIA DGX Spark machines (one GB10 GPU and 128 GB of memory each), linked by 200 GbE RoCE. I ran it there with the stock vLLM 0.32.0 image:

CheckPro NVFP4, four DGX Sparks
17 × 23391
10 word problems, thinking on10/10
8 short factual questions8/8
Tool callcorrect
Click targets on five synthetic screenshots (the same plain prompt as above; not a grounding benchmark)5/5 inside the target
A fact hidden in a prompt of about 25,000 tokensfound
One stream, 512 tokens, prefill included24.1 tok/s

It loaded in about ten minutes from a network share, and vLLM chose the same Marlin FP4 kernel as on the RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000 in the earlier tests. The sampled weight error after quantization is 9.2% on average and 9.6% at most (one expert in 64 measured in each of the 120 files that hold experts), against Mini's 9.5%. Weight error alone does not predict the damage, though: Nano had the same error as Mini and still lost grounding accuracy. My expectation that Pro's quantization costs as little as Mini's rests on their shared design, a mixture of experts quantized the same way, and that is an inference, not a measurement of Pro.

I then ran the same ScreenSpot-Pro benchmark on Pro, with exactly the requests used for Mini and Nano. It scored 68.56% (1,084 of 1,581): 82.7% on text targets and 45.7% on icons. Question by question that is 6.5 points better than Mini's quantization (95% interval 4.3 to 8.7 points; exact McNemar p < 0.001). The run took most of an afternoon, because the Sparks reached my temperature limits (GPU 86 °C, SoC 93 °C) every few minutes and the benchmark paused again and again to let them cool.

Twice as fast with a drafter (added 2026-11-06)

Speculative decoding makes generation faster without changing which model answers: a small drafter proposes several tokens, and the big model checks them all in one step, keeping the ones it agrees with. The usual drafter for a Qwen3.5 model is its own multi-token-prediction (MTP) layer, but the NorthCUA checkpoints ship without it: their configs set mtp_num_hidden_layers to 0 and contain no MTP weights. So I tried three replacements on each model, on the same eight requests (four computer-use steps with a screenshot and the Harness's click tool, two word problems, a short function and a copy-edit task), greedy, one request at a time:

Model, hardwareWithout drafterBase model's MTP layer, grafted backPrompt lookup (n-gram)DFlash drafter, 7 tokens
Nano, one RTX PRO 6000158 tok/s1.08×1.07×2.25×
Mini, one RTX PRO 6000182 tok/s1.02×1.13×1.86×
Pro, four DGX Sparks24.4 tok/snot triednot tried2.03×

The MTP layer from the base Qwen3.5 checkpoints loads cleanly once grafted back (I fetched only those tensors and quantized its experts like the rest), but its drafts were mostly rejected: it was trained on the base model's hidden states, and the fine-tune moved them. The DFlash drafters published by z-lab for the base models did much better, although they were not trained on NorthCUA's outputs either. With eight requests in flight the gain shrinks (1.68× for Nano, 1.34× for Mini), and it is smallest on computer-use steps, whose output is short and specific: 1.2 to 1.7× on Nano, 1.0 to 1.2× on Mini and 1.4 to 1.75× on Pro. Word problems and code gain 2 to 3.5×, copying text 4 to 5×.

Speculative decoding is not bit-for-bit neutral: verifying several tokens at once uses slightly different GPU arithmetic, so a greedy answer can change where two tokens are nearly tied. Without the drafter, the same request always gave the same text. So I reran the three benchmarks on Mini and Nano with the drafter on. Nothing changed significantly: Mini scored 61.10% on ScreenSpot-Pro (62.05% without; paired p 0.20), 85.44% on GSM8K (87.04%; p 0.11) and 78.74% on IFEval (the same), and Nano 14.23% (13.73%; p 0.13), 81.20% (81.65%; p 0.39) and 67.47% (68.95%; p 0.27). On Pro I measured only the speed. Each model card now has the one-line vLLM option.

Using them

Each model card has a vLLM command and Python examples that I ran against the served models: a screenshot question, a request with thinking on, and a tool call. For computer use, run the models with the official NorthCUA Harness, and keep every GUI coordinate in the 0–1000 grid the models were trained with.

On other engines: these checkpoints are tested on vLLM only. SGLang reads compressed-tensors checkpoints but has not been tried with this layout yet. llama.cpp and Ollama load GGUF files instead, and GGUF quantizations of Nano and Mini already exist (linked from their cards). TensorRT-LLM's NVFP4 support is built around NVIDIA's own ModelOpt checkpoint layout, and I have not tried it with these files.

I posted a short note about each quantization in the NorthCUA team's community tab: Nano, Mini and Pro.
